questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Vertical Hyperbola Given Graphically
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068362/assets/432f8963425031983284db54310c8ae604bc993de66494dceb48e6a4e2bcdf73.png)

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm \frac{7}{6}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0,\pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,-7)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=7.$

Recall also that the asymptotes of the hyperbola occur at $y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{7}{6}x.
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =\frac{7}{6} \\ \frac{7}{b} & =\frac{7}{6} \\ b & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=6\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=7\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

are given by

x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
questions.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sec}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{\sqrt{5}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{5} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{5}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{5} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Parametrizing Part of a Vertical Hyperbola
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068362/assets/32375f839dd0f51a8624bebda732d7413130c940045db7e5a1a9fce3576e91b6.png)

One branch of a hyperbola (shown above) is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $t?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

$$
x=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a single branch, we refer to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068362/assets/d44195c764b2943c3d5b5e0d91ee770011c951d7a825f0c5cc4d1f38cedbb709.png)

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $(-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}),$ we get only the upper branch.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe only the upper branch are

$$
x=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$
